content: The genus Aesculus consists of 20 to 25 species of deciduous trees and shrubs that are native to the temperate regions of the Northern Hemisphere. Among these, 7 to 10 species are native to North America, while 13 to 15 species are found in Eurasia. Additionally, several natural hybrids exist within this genus. Historically, these plants were classified in their own family, Hippocastanaceae, which was typically considered monogeneric. However, genetic evidence has led to the inclusion of this family, along with the Aceraceae (maples and Dipteronia), within the soapberry family, Sapindaceae. In North America, species of Aesculus are commonly referred to as buckeyes, while in Eurasia, they are known as horse-chestnuts. Some species are also called white chestnut or red chestnut, as seen in certain Bach flower remedies. In Britain, these trees are sometimes colloquially referred to as conker trees due to their association with the traditional children's game of conkers. The term horse-chestnut is hyphenated to distinguish it from true chestnuts (Castanea, family Fagaceae). The name horse-chestnut is often written as Horse Chestnut or Horsechestnut. One particularly popular species in cultivation, the common horse-chestnut (Aesculus hippocastanum), is frequently referred to simply as horse-chestnut. The genus name Aesculus was assigned by Linnaeus, derived from the Roman name for an edible acorn. The use of the term horse in the name does not imply suitability as horse fodder, as suggested by folk etymology, but rather refers to the strength or inedibility of the seeds. The name buckeye originates from the resemblance of the seed to the brown eye of a male deer (buck), while horse-chestnut refers to the external similarity of the seed to a chestnut, despite being inedible. Buckeyes typically bloom in summer, whereas horse-chestnuts flower in late spring. Description Aesculus species are woody plants that range in height from 4 to 35 meters, depending on the species. They are characterized by stout shoots with resinous, often sticky buds. The leaves are opposite and palmately divided, often very large, with some species, such as the Japanese horse-chestnut (Aesculus turbinata), having leaves up to 65 cm across. The flowers are showy and insect-pollinated, with a single fouror five-lobed petal (technically four or five petals fused at the base). Flowering begins after 80 to 110 growing degree days. The fruit is a glossy, rich brown to blackish-brown nut, 2 to 5 cm in diameter, usually globose, and encased in a green or brown husk. Typically, there is one nut per husk, but occasionally two nuts may develop within a single husk, in which case the nuts are flattened on one side. The point of attachment of the nut within the husk is marked by a large circular whitish scar. The husk may have scattered soft spines in some species, while others are spineless. The husk splits into three sections to release the nut. Cultivation The most widely recognized member of the genus is the common horse-chestnut (Aesculus hippocastanum), which is native to a small region in the Balkans of southeastern Europe but is extensively cultivated throughout temperate regions worldwide. The yellow buckeye (Aesculus flava, synonym A. octandra) is another valuable ornamental tree with yellow flowers, though it is less commonly planted. Among the smaller species, the bottlebrush buckeye (Aesculus parviflora) is notable for its unique and striking flowering shrub form. Several other species within the genus are also used as ornamentals, and numerous horticultural hybrids have been developed. One notable hybrid is the red horse-chestnut (A. × carnea), a cross between A. hippocastanum and A. pavia. These trees are generally low-maintenance and relatively problem-free. However, a recently discovered leaf-mining moth (Cameraria ohridella) has caused significant issues across much of Europe, leading to premature leaf drop and an unattractive appearance. The symptoms, which include brown blotches on the leaves, can be mistaken for damage caused by the leaf fungus Guignardia aesculi, which is also common but typically less severe. The common horse-chestnut also serves as a food source for the larvae of the sycamore moth, another species of moth. Another disease affecting Aesculus species in parts of northwestern Europe and North America is bleeding canker. Uses The nuts of Aesculus species contain high concentrations of a saponin-class toxin called aesculin, which is toxic to many animals, including humans, as it causes hemolysis (destruction of red blood cells). The saponin can be removed by leaching the pulverized nuts in multiple changes of boiling water, yielding a starchy porridge that was once an important food source for some Native American tribes. Certain animals, such as deer and squirrels, are resistant to the toxins and can consume the nuts directly. Interestingly, aesculin is a natural pH indicator that changes from colorless to fluorescent blue under UV light in an acidic pH range. Crushed buckeye nuts have also been used by poachers, who throw them into lakes to kill fish for easy capture. The California buckeye (Aesculus californica) is known to produce toxic nectar that can poison honeybees, although other native bee species in the area are unaffected. Other buckeye species are believed to have similar effects, but the toxins are diluted due to the trees' limited abundance in any given area. The wood of Aesculus species is pale whitish-brown, relatively soft, and not widely used. It has been employed for making inexpensive furniture, boxes, and firewood. In several European countries, a new disease has been identified in various Aesculus species. In Britain and Ireland, the game of conkers remains a popular childhood pastime. In some cultures, the buckeye tree is considered a symbol of good luck. The Mexican buckeye, while related to Aesculus, belongs to a separate genus, Ungnadia.
